```{python}
#| echo: false
import subprocess
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import HTML

def render_tikz(tikz_code: str, scale: float = 1.25) -> HTML:
    """Compiles a TikZ snippet to an inline SVG using latex + dvisvgm."""
    tex_doc = f"""\\documentclass[dvisvgm,tikz,border=6pt]{{standalone}}
\\usepackage{{amsmath,amssymb}}
\\usepackage{{tikz}}
\\begin{{document}}
{tikz_code}
\\end{{document}}
"""
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
        tmp_path = Path(tmpdir)
        tex_file = tmp_path / "diagram.tex"
        dvi_file = tmp_path / "diagram.dvi"
        svg_file = tmp_path / "diagram.svg"
        tex_file.write_text(tex_doc, encoding="utf-8")

        subprocess.run(
            ["latex", "-interaction=nonstopmode", "-halt-on-error", "diagram.tex"],
            cwd=tmpdir,
            check=True,
            stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
        )
        subprocess.run(
            ["dvisvgm", "--no-fonts", f"-Z {scale}", "diagram.dvi", "-o", "diagram.svg"],
            cwd=tmpdir,
            check=True,
            stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
        )
        svg_content = svg_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    return HTML(f'<div style="text-align: center; margin: 1.2rem 0;">{svg_content}</div>')
```

## Fundamental Quantities of Mechanics

Engineering mechanics relies on four basic quantities:

* **Length:** Used to locate the position of a point in space and describe the size of a physical system; once a standard unit of length is defined, distances and geometric properties of a body are expressed as multiples of this unit.
* **Time:** Conceived as a succession of events; while the principles of statics are time-independent, time plays an important role in dynamics.
* **Mass:** A measure of a quantity of matter used to compare the action of one body with another; it manifests as gravitational attraction between two bodies and measures the resistance of matter to a change in velocity.
* **Force:** Considered as a "push" or "pull" exerted by one body on another, occurring either through direct contact (such as pushing on a wall) or through a distance when physically separated (such as gravitational, electrical, and magnetic forces). A force is completely characterized by its **magnitude**, **direction**, and **point of application**.

---

## From 2D to 3D Rectangular Components

### 2D Review vs. 3D Extension

In two dimensions, a vector $\mathbf{A}$ making an angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis is resolved into rectangular components using simple right-triangle trigonometry:

$$A_x = A \cos\theta, \quad A_y = A \sin\theta$$

$$\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{} = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}, \quad \angle\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right)$$

In three dimensions, vector algebra operations are greatly simplified by expressing vectors in **Cartesian vector form**.

### Right-Handed Coordinate System

We use a **right-handed coordinate system** where the positive $z$-axis is directed upward (the zenith direction) to measure height or altitude, while the $x$ and $y$ axes lie in the horizontal plane. A rectangular coordinate system is right-handed if the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of the positive $z$-axis when the right-hand fingers are curled about this axis from the positive $x$-axis toward the positive $y$-axis.

::: {.callout-warning}
### Watch Your Axis Orientation!
Swapping the positive $x$ and $y$ axes so that curling your fingers from $+x$ to $+y$ points your thumb downward creates a left-handed coordinate system, which is **wrong** for our vector formulations. Always verify your axes using the right-hand rule before reading coordinates.
:::

{{< video assets/videos/Scene01_2Dvs3DRightHandRule.mp4 >}}

### Rectangular & Cartesian Vector Representation

When a vector $\mathbf{A}$ is directed within an octant of the $x, y, z$ frame, two successive applications of the parallelogram law resolve the vector first into $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}' + \mathbf{A}_z$ (where $\mathbf{A}'$ is the projection in the $xy$-plane) and then $\mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A}_x + \mathbf{A}_y$, yielding the vector sum:

$$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}_x + \mathbf{A}_y + \mathbf{A}_z$$

::: {.callout-important}
### TA Note: Separate Magnitude and Direction
Writing $A = A_x + A_y + A_z$ as a scalar sum is **not accurate** because each component has both a magnitude and a distinct axis direction. Using the Cartesian unit vectors $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$ along the positive $x, y, z$ axes separates the scalar magnitude ($A_x, A_y, A_z$) from the direction ($\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$):

$$\mathbf{A} = A_x\mathbf{i} + A_y\mathbf{j} + A_z\mathbf{k}$$
:::

### Magnitude of a Cartesian Vector

From the two right triangles formed by the 3D parallelepiped, $A = \sqrt{A'^2 + A_z^2}$ and $A' = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$. Combining these equations to eliminate $A'$ gives the magnitude of $\mathbf{A}$ as the positive square root of the sum of the squares of its components:

$$\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{} = A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$$

{{< video assets/videos/Scene02_CartesianParallelepiped.mp4 >}}

## Direction Cosines & Unit Vectors

### Coordinate Direction Angles ($\alpha, \beta, \gamma$)

The direction of a Cartesian vector $\mathbf{A}$ is defined by the **coordinate direction angles** $\alpha$ (alpha), $\beta$ (beta), and $\gamma$ (gamma)—also abbreviated as $\theta_x = \alpha$, $\theta_y = \beta$, and $\theta_z = \gamma$—measured between the tail of $\mathbf{A}$ and the positive $x, y, z$ axes located at the tail of $\mathbf{A}$. Regardless of where $\mathbf{A}$ is directed, each angle lies between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.

Projecting $\mathbf{A}$ onto the $x, y, z$ axes forms three right triangles that define the **direction cosines** of $\mathbf{A}$:

$$\cos\alpha = \frac{A_x}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}, \quad \cos\beta = \frac{A_y}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}, \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{A_z}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}$$

Note also that if the angle $\gamma$ with the $z$-axis is given, the intermediate projection onto the $xy$-plane has magnitude $A' = A\sin\gamma$.

### Unit Vector ($\mathbf{u}_A$) and Direction Cosine Identity

Dividing $\mathbf{A}$ by its magnitude $\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}$ produces a dimensionless **unit vector** $\mathbf{u}_A$ of magnitude $1$ pointing in the direction of $\mathbf{A}$:

$$\mathbf{u}_A = \frac{\mathbf{A}}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}} = \frac{A_x}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\mathbf{i} + \frac{A_y}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\mathbf{j} + \frac{A_z}{\vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}}\mathbf{k} = \cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + \cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + \cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}$$

Because the magnitude of $\mathbf{u}_A$ is equal to $1$, the sum of the squares of the direction cosines satisfies the fundamental identity:

$$\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$$

If any two of the coordinate direction angles are known, the third angle can be found using this equation. Furthermore, if the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of $\mathbf{A}$ are known, $\mathbf{A}$ is expressed in Cartesian vector form as:

$$\mathbf{A} = \vert{}\mathbf{A}\vert{}\cdot\mathbf{u}_A = A\cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + A\cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + A\cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}$$

{{< video assets/videos/Scene03_DirectionCosinesAndUnitVector.mp4 >}}

## Position Vectors & Force Along a Line

A **position vector** $\mathbf{r}$ is a fixed vector that locates a point in space relative to another point:

1. **From the Origin ($O$ to $P$):** If $\mathbf{r}$ extends from the origin of coordinates $O(0,0,0)$ to a point $P(x, y, z)$, then:
   $$\mathbf{r} = P - O = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + z\mathbf{k}$$
   For example, starting at $O$, measuring $x_A = +4\text{ m}$, $y_A = +2\text{ m}$, and $z_A = -6\text{ m}$ locates $A(4\text{ m}, 2\text{ m}, -6\text{ m})$, while $B(6\text{ m}, -1\text{ m}, 4\text{ m})$ is located at $x_B = +6\text{ m}$, $y_B = -1\text{ m}$, and $z_B = +4\text{ m}$.
2. **Between Two Points ($A$ to $B$):** For a position vector directed from an initial point $A(x_A, y_A, z_A)$ to a terminal point $B(x_B, y_B, z_B)$ (or from $P$ to $Q$), head-to-tail triangle addition requires $\mathbf{r}_A + \mathbf{r}_{AB} = \mathbf{r}_B$, giving the difference between the two points ("destination minus origin"):
   $$\mathbf{r}_{AB} = \mathbf{r}_B - \mathbf{r}_A = (x_B - x_A)\mathbf{i} + (y_B - y_A)\mathbf{j} + (z_B - z_A)\mathbf{k}$$

To express a force $\mathbf{F}$ of known magnitude $F$ directed along a cable or line from $A$ to $B$, multiply the scalar magnitude $F$ by the unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{AB} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_{AB}}{\vert{}\mathbf{r}_{AB}\vert{}}$.

{{< video assets/videos/Scene04_PositionVectors.mp4 >}}

## Worked Lecture Examples

### Example 1: Force Directed Along a Cable

**Problem:** A cable attached to an eyebolt at $A(4\text{ m}, 0, 3\text{ m})$ is pulled toward point $B(0, 6\text{ m}, 0)$ with a force $\mathbf{F}$ of magnitude $500\text{ N}$. Determine the rectangular representation of this force.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.75, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (5.5,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,7.2,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,4.2) node[above] {$z$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0,0) {$O$};

  % Parallelepiped construction lines
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,0,3) -- (4,0,3) -- (4,0,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,0,3) -- (0,6,3) -- (0,6,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (4,0,0) -- (4,6,0) -- (0,6,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (4,0,3) -- (4,6,3) -- (0,6,3);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (4,6,0) -- (4,6,3);

  % Dimension labels
  \node[above left, font=\footnotesize] at (2,0,3) {$4\text{ m}$};
  \node[left, font=\footnotesize] at (4,0,1.5) {$3\text{ m}$};
  \node[above, font=\footnotesize] at (0,3,3) {$6\text{ m}$};

  % Line of action AB and Force Vector F
  \draw[dashed, thick, blue!50!black] (4,0,3) -- (0,6,0);
  \draw[->, ultra thick, blue!80!black] (4,0,3) -- (2.2,2.7,1.65) node[above right] {$\mathbf{F} = 500\text{ N}$};

  % Points A and B
  \filldraw[black] (4,0,3) circle (2pt) node[left] {$A(4,0,3)$};
  \filldraw[black] (0,6,0) circle (2pt) node[below right] {$B(0,6,0)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

1. **Write the position vector $\vec{AB}$ from $A$ to $B$ in rectangular form:** Avoid common errors (choosing the wrong signs or mixing up scalar components) by sketching the parallelepiped from $A$ to $B$:
   $$\vec{AB} = -4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}\text{ m}$$

2. **Evaluate the unit vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda} = \mathbf{u}_{AB}$ from $A$ toward $B$:**
   $$\mathbf{u}_{AB} = \boldsymbol{\lambda} = \frac{\vec{AB}}{\vert{}\vec{AB}\vert{}} = \frac{-4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{(-4)^2 + 6^2 + (-3)^2}} = -0.5122\mathbf{i} + 0.7682\mathbf{j} - 0.3841\mathbf{k}$$

3. **Multiply by the magnitude of the force ($F = 500\text{ N}$):**
   $$\mathbf{F} = F\boldsymbol{\lambda} = 500(-0.5122\mathbf{i} + 0.7682\mathbf{j} - 0.3841\mathbf{k}) = \{-256\mathbf{i} + 384\mathbf{j} - 192\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}$$

---

### Example 2: Force from Coordinate Direction Angles

**Problem:** Express the force $F = 200\text{ N}$ acting in the first octant with $\beta = 60^\circ$ and $\gamma = 45^\circ$ as a Cartesian vector.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.95, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (4.0,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,4.0,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,4.0) node[above] {$z$};

  % Projection lines
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2,0,0) -- (2,2,0) -- (0,2,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2,2,0) -- (2,2,2.83);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,0,0) -- (2,2,0);

  % Force vector F
  \draw[->, ultra thick, red!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (2,2,2.83) node[above right] {$\mathbf{F} = 200\text{ N}$};

  % Direction angle arcs
  \draw[->, blue!70!black, thick] (0,0,1.3) to[bend left=20] node[above, font=\footnotesize] {$\gamma = 45^\circ$} (0.75,0.75,1.06);
  \draw[->, green!50!black, thick] (0,1.4,0) to[bend right=20] node[right, font=\footnotesize] {$\beta = 60^\circ$} (0.85,0.85,1.2);
  \draw[->, orange!80!black, thick] (1.6,0,0) to[bend left=25] node[left, font=\footnotesize] {$\alpha$} (0.95,0.95,1.34);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

1. **Find the unknown coordinate direction angle $\alpha$:** Using the direction cosine identity:
   $$\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \implies \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2 45^\circ = 1$$

   *(Note: The lecture slide contains a typographical error printing $\cos^2 0^\circ$ and $(0)^2$ in the intermediate substitution line instead of $\cos^2 60^\circ = (0.5)^2$, though its final root $\pm 0.5$ is based on $\beta = 60^\circ$.)*
   $$\cos\alpha = \sqrt{1 - (0.5)^2 - (0.707)^2} = \pm 0.5 \implies \alpha = \cos^{-1}(0.5) = 60^\circ \text{ or } \cos^{-1}(-0.5) = 120^\circ$$

   Because the force vector points in the positive $x$ direction, we select $\alpha = 60^\circ$.
2. **Express $\mathbf{F}$ in Cartesian vector form:**
   $$\mathbf{F} = F\cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i} + F\cos\beta\,\mathbf{j} + F\cos\gamma\,\mathbf{k}$$

   $$\mathbf{F} = (200\cos 60^\circ\text{ N})\mathbf{i} + (200\cos 60^\circ\text{ N})\mathbf{j} + (200\cos 45^\circ\text{ N})\mathbf{k} = \{100.0\mathbf{i} + 100.0\mathbf{j} + 141.4\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}$$

### Example 3: Double-Projection Resolution ($A_{xy}$ Method)

**Problem:** For the position vector $\mathbf{A}$ of magnitude $A = 12\text{ m}$ making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the positive $z$-axis and whose projection in the $xy$-plane makes an angle of $40^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis toward the positive $y$-axis, determine (1) the rectangular representation of $\mathbf{A}$ and (2) the angles between $\mathbf{A}$ and each of the positive coordinate axes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.85, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Shaded vertical projection plane
  \fill[blue!8] (0,0,0) -- (2.3,1.93,0) -- (2.3,1.93,3.8) -- cycle;

  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (4.2,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,4.2,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,4.6) node[above] {$z$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0,0) {$O$};

  % Projections in xy plane
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.3,0,0) -- (2.3,1.93,0) -- (0,1.93,0);
  \draw[dashed, thick, green!50!black] (0,0,0) -- (2.3,1.93,0) node[below right, font=\footnotesize] {$A_{xy}$};
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.3,1.93,0) -- (2.3,1.93,3.8);

  % Vector A
  \draw[->, ultra thick, blue!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (2.3,1.93,3.8) node[above right] {$\mathbf{A} \; (12\text{ m})$};

  % Angles
  \draw[->, thick, red!70!black] (0,0,1.6) to[bend left=20] node[above right, font=\footnotesize] {$30^\circ$} (0.75,0.63,1.25);
  \draw[->, thick, orange!80!black] (1.5,0,0) to[bend right=20] node[below, font=\footnotesize] {$40^\circ$} (1.15,0.96,0);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

1. **Resolve $\mathbf{A}$ into vertical ($A_z$) and horizontal ($A_{xy}$) components, then resolve $A_{xy}$ into $A_x$ and $A_y$:**
   $$A_z = A\cos 30^\circ = 12\cos 30^\circ = 10.392\text{ m}$$

   $$A_{xy} = A\sin 30^\circ = 12\sin 30^\circ = 6\text{ m}$$

   $$A_x = A_{xy}\cos 40^\circ = 6\cos 40^\circ = 4.596\text{ m}$$

   $$A_y = A_{xy}\sin 40^\circ = 6\sin 40^\circ = 3.857\text{ m}$$

   $$\mathbf{A} = A_x\mathbf{i} + A_y\mathbf{j} + A_z\mathbf{k} = \{4.60\mathbf{i} + 3.86\mathbf{j} + 10.39\mathbf{k}\}\text{ m}$$

2. **Calculate the coordinate direction angles ($\theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z$):**
   $$\theta_x = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_x}{A}\right) = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4.596}{12}\right) = 67.5^\circ$$

   $$\theta_y = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_y}{A}\right) = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3.857}{12}\right) = 71.3^\circ$$

   $$\theta_z = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_z}{A}\right) = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{10.392}{12}\right) = 30.0^\circ$$

---

### Example 4: Obtuse Coordinate Direction Angles

**Problem:** Express the force $F = 500\text{ N}$ (directed in the $+x, -y, -z$ octant, making $45^\circ$ with the negative $y$-axis and $60^\circ$ with the negative $z$-axis) as a Cartesian vector.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.8, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Axes (+ and -)
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (4.2,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,2.5,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[dashed, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,-4.0,0) node[left] {$-y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,2.2) node[above] {$z$};
  \draw[dashed, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,-3.5) node[below] {$-z$};

  % Parallelepiped in (+x, -y, -z) octant
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.5,0,0) -- (2.5,-3.2,0) -- (0,-3.2,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,-3.2,0) -- (0,-3.2,-2.5) -- (0,0,-2.5);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.5,0,0) -- (2.5,0,-2.5) -- (0,0,-2.5);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.5,-3.2,0) -- (2.5,-3.2,-2.5);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,-3.2,-2.5) -- (2.5,-3.2,-2.5) -- (2.5,0,-2.5);

  % Force vector F
  \draw[->, ultra thick, red!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (2.5,-3.2,-2.5) node[below left] {$\mathbf{F} = 500\text{ N}$};

  % Angles with -y and -z
  \draw[->, blue!70!black, thick] (0,-1.6,0) to[bend right=20] node[above left, font=\footnotesize] {$45^\circ$} (1.0,-1.28,-1.0);
  \draw[->, green!50!black, thick] (0,0,-1.5) to[bend left=20] node[right, font=\footnotesize] {$60^\circ$} (1.0,-1.28,-1.0);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

1. **Determine the coordinate direction angles from the positive axes:** Since the vector makes $45^\circ$ with $-y$ and $60^\circ$ with $-z$, the supplementary angles measured from the positive $y$ and $z$ axes are $\beta = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ$ and $\gamma = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$.
   $$\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2 135^\circ + \cos^2 120^\circ = 1 \implies \alpha = 60^\circ$$

2. **Write the Cartesian vector:**
   $$\mathbf{F} = F\mathbf{u}_F = (500\text{ N})(0.5\mathbf{i} - 0.7071\mathbf{j} - 0.5\mathbf{k}) = \{250\mathbf{i} - 354\mathbf{j} - 250\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}$$

## Guided Tutorial Practice Problems (Problems 1–4)

### Problem 1
**Statement:** Obtain the rectangular representation of the force $\mathbf{P}$, given that its magnitude is $30\text{ N}$, it is inclined at $50^\circ$ above its projection in the $xy$-plane, and its $xy$-plane projection makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the $+y$ axis toward the $-x$ axis.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.85, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Shaded vertical triangle
  \fill[cyan!12] (0,0,0) -- (-1.6,2.77,0) -- (-1.6,2.77,3.4) -- cycle;

  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (3.2,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[dashed, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (-2.5,0,0) node[above right] {$-x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,4.2,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,4.2) node[above] {$z$};

  % Projection lines
  \draw[dashed, thick, gray!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (-1.6,2.77,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (-1.6,2.77,0) -- (-1.6,2.77,3.4);

  % Force P
  \draw[->, ultra thick, blue!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (-1.6,2.77,3.4) node[above] {$\mathbf{P} = 30\text{ N}$};

  % Angle arcs
  \draw[->, red!75!black, thick] (-0.75,1.3,0) to[bend right=15] node[left, font=\footnotesize] {$50^\circ$} (-0.65,1.12,1.38);
  \draw[->, green!50!black, thick] (0,1.8,0) to[bend right=20] node[above right, font=\footnotesize] {$30^\circ$} (-0.9,1.56,0);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

* Project $\mathbf{P}$ onto the $z$-axis and the $xy$-plane:
  $$P_z = 30\sin 50^\circ = 22.98\text{ N} \approx 23\text{ N}$$

  $$P_{xy} = 30\cos 50^\circ = 19.28\text{ N}$$
* Resolve $P_{xy}$ along the $-x$ and $+y$ axes:
  $$P_x = -P_{xy}\sin 30^\circ = -19.28(0.5) = -9.64\text{ N}$$
  $$P_y = P_{xy}\cos 30^\circ = 19.28(0.8660) = 16.70\text{ N}$$
  $$\mathbf{P} = \{-9.64\mathbf{i} + 16.70\mathbf{j} + 22.98\mathbf{k}\}\text{ N}$$

::: {.callout-note}
### TA Caution on Slide Annotations
The handwritten annotation on the lecture slide lists $P_x = -15$, $P_y = 15\sqrt{3}$, and $P_z = 23$. Notice that $-15 = -30\sin 30^\circ$ and $15\sqrt{3} = 30\cos 30^\circ$, which resolves the full $30\text{ N}$ magnitude directly in the $xy$-plane without first multiplying by $\cos 50^\circ$! Always project onto the $xy$-plane ($P_{xy} = P\cos 50^\circ$) before resolving into $x$ and $y$ components.
:::

### Problem 2
**Statement:** The force $\mathbf{F}$ acts on the bracket within the octant shown. If $F = 400\text{ N}$, $\beta = 60^\circ$, and $\gamma = 45^\circ$, determine the $x, y, z$ components of $\mathbf{F}$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.85, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (3.2,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[dashed, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (-2.8,0,0) node[above left] {$-x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,4.2,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,4.2) node[above] {$z$};

  % Projections in (-x, +y, +z) octant
  \draw[dashed, gray] (-2,0,0) -- (-2,2.2,0) -- (0,2.2,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (-2,2.2,0) -- (-2,2.2,2.9);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,0,0) -- (-2,2.2,0);

  % Force F
  \draw[->, ultra thick, red!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (-2,2.2,2.9) node[above right] {$\mathbf{F} = 400\text{ N}$};

  % Angles alpha, beta, gamma
  \draw[->, blue!75!black, thick] (0,0,1.5) to[bend left=20] node[above left, font=\footnotesize] {$\gamma = 45^\circ$} (-0.75,0.82,1.08);
  \draw[->, green!50!black, thick] (0,1.6,0) to[bend right=20] node[right, font=\footnotesize] {$\beta = 60^\circ$} (-0.85,0.93,1.23);
  \draw[->, orange!80!black, thick] (1.3,0,0) to[bend left=30] node[below right, font=\footnotesize] {$\alpha$} (-0.65,0.72,0.95);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

* Using $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$:
  $$\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2 45^\circ = 1 \implies \cos\alpha = \pm 0.5$$
* Since $\mathbf{F}$ is directed into the $-x, +y, +z$ octant ($\alpha = 120^\circ$), $\cos\alpha = -0.5$ (magnitude $\vert{}F_x\vert{} = 200\text{ N}$):
  $$F_x = -400(0.5) = -200\text{ N} \quad (\text{magnitude } 200\text{ N})$$
  $$F_y = 400\cos 60^\circ = 200\text{ N}$$
  $$F_z = 400\cos 45^\circ = 282.843\text{ N}$$

### Problem 3
**Statement:** Determine the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of $\mathbf{F}_2$ so that the resultant of the two forces ($\mathbf{F}_1 = 180\text{ N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$) acts along the positive $x$-axis and has a magnitude of $500\text{ N}$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.85, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Shaded projection triangles for F1
  \fill[cyan!18] (0,0,0) -- (2.6,1.5,0) -- (0,3.0,0) -- cycle;
  \fill[cyan!10] (0,0,0) -- (2.6,1.5,0) -- (2.6,1.5,-1.0) -- cycle;

  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (4.5,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,4.2,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,3.8) node[above] {$z$};

  % Projection lines for F1
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,0,0) -- (2.6,1.5,0) -- (2.6,1.5,-1.0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.6,0,0) -- (2.6,1.5,0) -- (0,1.5,0);

  % Force F1
  \draw[->, ultra thick, blue!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (2.6,1.5,-1.0) node[below right] {$\mathbf{F}_1 = 180\text{ N}$};

  % Force F2
  \draw[->, ultra thick, red!80!black] (0,0,0) -- (2.4,-2.0,2.2) node[above left] {$\mathbf{F}_2$};

  % Angles for F1
  \draw[->, green!50!black, thick] (0,1.4,0) to[bend left=20] node[above right, font=\footnotesize] {$60^\circ$} (1.2,0.7,0);
  \draw[->, orange!80!black, thick] (1.9,1.1,0) to[bend left=15] node[left, font=\footnotesize] {$15^\circ$} (1.9,1.1,-0.73);

  % Direction angles for F2
  \draw[->, purple!80!black, thick] (0,0,1.3) to[bend right=20] node[above left, font=\footnotesize] {$\gamma_2$} (0.8,-0.67,0.73);
  \draw[->, purple!80!black, thick] (1.4,0,0) to[bend left=20] node[left, font=\footnotesize] {$\alpha_2$} (1.0,-0.83,0.92);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

1. **Resolve $\mathbf{F}_1 = 180\text{ N}$ into components:** $\mathbf{F}_1$ is inclined $15^\circ$ below the $xy$-plane along a projection line $60^\circ$ from the $+y$ axis toward the $+x$ axis:
   $$F_{1x} = (180\cos 15^\circ)\sin 60^\circ = 150.57\text{ N}$$
   $$F_{1y} = (180\cos 15^\circ)\cos 60^\circ = 86.93\text{ N}$$
   $$F_{1z} = -180\sin 15^\circ = -46.59\text{ N}$$
2. **Apply $\mathbf{F}_R = \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 = 500\mathbf{i}\text{ N}$:**
   $$F_{2x} = 500 - 150.57 = 349.43\text{ N}$$
   $$F_{2y} = 0 - 86.93 = -86.93\text{ N}$$
   $$F_{2z} = 0 - (-46.59) = 46.59\text{ N}$$
3. **Compute the magnitude and coordinate direction angles of $\mathbf{F}_2$:**
   $$F_2 = \sqrt{(349.43)^2 + (-86.93)^2 + (46.59)^2} = 363.1\text{ N}$$
   $$\alpha_2 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{349.43}{363.1}\right) = 15.8^\circ, \quad \beta_2 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-86.93}{363.1}\right) = 103.9^\circ, \quad \gamma_2 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{46.59}{363.1}\right) = 82.6^\circ$$

### Problem 4
**Statement:** The pole is subjected to the force $\mathbf{F}$ which has components $F_x = 1.5\text{ kN}$ and $F_z = 1.25\text{ kN}$. If $\beta = 75^\circ$, determine the magnitudes of $\mathbf{F}$ and $F_y$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
render_tikz(r"""
\begin{tikzpicture}[x={(-0.55cm,-0.42cm)}, y={(1cm,0cm)}, z={(0cm,1cm)}, scale=0.85, >=stealth, line cap=round, line join=round, font=\small]
  % Vertical Pole below origin
  \draw[line width=6pt, blue!25!gray] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,-2.2);

  % Axes
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (4.2,0,0) node[below left] {$x$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,4.2,0) node[right] {$y$};
  \draw[->, thick, gray!70!black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,4.0) node[above] {$z$};

  % Parallelepiped
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.6,0,0) -- (2.6,2.2,0) -- (0,2.2,0);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,0,2.3) -- (2.6,0,2.3) -- (2.6,2.2,2.3) -- (0,2.2,2.3) -- cycle;
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.6,0,0) -- (2.6,0,2.3);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (2.6,2.2,0) -- (2.6,2.2,2.3);
  \draw[dashed, gray] (0,2.2,0) -- (0,2.2,2.3);

  % Component Vectors Fx, Fy, Fz
  \draw[->, very thick, black] (0,0,0) -- (2.6,0,0) node[above left] {$\mathbf{F}_x = 1.5\text{ kN}$};
  \draw[->, very thick, black] (0,0,0) -- (0,2.2,0) node[above right] {$\mathbf{F}_y$};
  \draw[->, very thick, black] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,2.3) node[left] {$\mathbf{F}_z = 1.25\text{ kN}$};

  % Resultant Vector F
  \draw[->, ultra thick, cyan!70!blue] (0,0,0) -- (2.6,2.2,2.3) node[above right] {$\mathbf{F}$};

  % Angle beta
  \draw[->, red!75!black, thick] (0,1.4,0) to[bend right=20] node[right, font=\footnotesize] {$\beta = 75^\circ$} (1.0,0.85,0.88);
\end{tikzpicture}
""")
```

**Solution:**

* Express $F_y$ in terms of $F$: $F_y = F\cos\beta = F\cos 75^\circ$.
* Substitute into the magnitude relation $F^2 = F_x^2 + F_y^2 + F_z^2$:
  $$F^2 = (1.5)^2 + (F\cos 75^\circ)^2 + (1.25)^2 \implies F^2(1 - \cos^2 75^\circ) = 3.8125$$
  $$F = \frac{\sqrt{3.8125}}{\sin 75^\circ} = 2.02\text{ kN}$$
  $$F_y = 2.021\cos 75^\circ = 0.523\text{ kN}$$
